about.title: Indigenous Religions of Australia and the Pacific
about.length_note: The class runs about 27 minutes, a little over the 25 aimed for. It covers six topics, and each one gets its own short steps and questions. You can pause between steps. The Pacific sections are brief tastes of a very large region, not full accounts.

say.text: Welcome to class fifteen. Today we visit Australia and the Pacific, and we describe each tradition the way its own people describe it.

show.text: Indigenous Religions of Australia and the Pacific

say.text: Three ideas will come back again and again: story, land and ancestors. We will take them one at a time.

show.text: Story · Land · Ancestors

say.text: Let's start in Australia. It has two distinct Indigenous peoples: Aboriginal peoples and Torres Strait Islander peoples.

show.text: Map of Australia. The mainland is marked Aboriginal peoples. The islands at the northern tip, near Papua New Guinea, are marked Torres Strait Islander peoples.

say.text: Within those two peoples there are hundreds of communities. Each has its own culture, customs, language and law.

show.text: Many communities, many traditions

say.text: So when we say Aboriginal spirituality, we mean many traditions, not one. Many of them speak of the Dreaming. In its stories, ancestral spirits created people and the natural world.

show.text: The Dreaming

say.text: The Dreaming is not only about the past. It joins past, present and future, and links people to the land and to each other.

show.text:
Past · Present · Future
People · Land · Each other

say.text: One more point. 'The Dreaming' is an English term for an Aboriginal idea. Each language group has its own word for it.

show.text: One English word, many Aboriginal words

ask.q: What is true about the word 'Dreaming'?
ask.right: It is an English term, and each Aboriginal language group has its own word for the idea.
wrong: It is one Aboriginal word that every group uses.
It is the title of a single holy book.
It only describes events in the distant past.
ask.why: Britannica Kids explains that 'The Dreaming' is the English term for an Aboriginal concept and that each language group has its own term. It is also not only about the past.

say.text: Now the second idea, land. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people use the word Country for it.

show.text: Country

say.text: Country is more than a place on a map. It is the land, the water, the animals, the plants and the people.

show.text: Land · Water · Animals · Plants · People

say.text: Places are tied to events in the Dreaming, so many are sacred sites. Connection to Country also brings responsibilities, set out in Aboriginal law and honoured through ceremony.

show.text:
Connection | Responsibility
Sacred sites tied to the Dreaming | Roles under Aboriginal law, honoured in ceremony

say.text: Here is an example. Uluru is a sacred site for the Anangu people. They say their ancestors made it in the Dreaming, on what had been a flat plain.

show.text: Uluru, a huge red rock rising from a flat desert plain, with caves and cracks along its sides.

ask.q: In the Anangu understanding, how did the features of Uluru come to be?
ask.right: Their ancestors created them during the Dreaming.
wrong: European surveyors built them in the 1800s.
A king had them carved for a temple.
Nobody has ever told a story about them.
ask.why: Britannica Kids reports that the Anangu believe their ancestors created the rock in the Dreaming. Their stories also explain its caves, cliffs, boulders and cracks.

say.text: Stories can tie land and ancestors together at a very large scale. Dreaming stories from the Great Barrier Reef region tell of ancestors who lived on land before the sea rose, more than 10,000 years ago.

show.text: A coral reef seen from above, with a faint outline of dry land beneath the shallow water.

say.text: Stories also work like maps. A songline, or Dreaming track, follows the route of ancestral beings as they travelled and created the land and its people.

show.text: A winding line crossing a desert map, with dots for places along the way where ancestors left parts of the story.

say.text: The Seven Sisters songlines are among the most extensive. An Aboriginal-led National Museum of Australia exhibition about them was created under the guidance of cultural custodians.

show.text: Seven Sisters songlines

ask.q: What does a songline, or Dreaming track, map?
ask.right: The routes ancestral beings took as they created the land and its people.
wrong: The roads built by early European explorers.
The borders of modern Australian states.
The routes of trading ships.
ask.why: The Museums of History NSW describes songlines as maps of the routes of Ancestral beings, who created the land and its people. They are pathways of knowledge.

say.text: Spirituality is not only spoken. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people express it through art, song, story, ceremony and the Dreaming.

show.text: Art · Song · Story · Ceremony

say.text: You may hear two phrases at events. A Welcome to Country can only be given by Traditional Owners who have their Elders' permission. An Acknowledgement of Country can be done by anyone.

show.text:
Welcome to Country | Acknowledgement of Country
Given by permitted Traditional Owners | Can be done by anyone in Australia

ask.q: Who can give a Welcome to Country?
ask.right: Traditional Owners who have been given permission by their Elders.
wrong: Any visitor who has read about the area.
Any government official.
Any teacher in a school.
ask.why: Study Australia says a Welcome to Country can only be delivered by Traditional Owners with permission from Elders. Anyone can do an Acknowledgement of Country.

say.text: Now to the Torres Strait Islands, between the tip of Cape York and Papua New Guinea. Torres Strait Islanders are a Melanesian sea-faring people, and they live on islands scattered across shallow seas.

show.text: The Torres Strait: more than 250 small islands between Cape York in Australia and Papua New Guinea. Fourteen are inhabited.

say.text: Their spirituality draws on the stories of Tagai. Tagai is a great fisherman and spirit being, and Islanders believe he created the world. He is seen as a constellation in the southern sky.

show.text: Tagai

say.text: In one Tagai story he stands in a canoe. In his left hand he holds a fishing spear, which is the Southern Cross. In his right hand he holds a red fruit called a sorbi.

show.text: A figure of stars shaped like a man standing in a canoe, with a spear in his left hand and a red fruit in his right.

say.text: In that story, Tagai and his crew of twelve were getting ready for a journey. Before it began, the crew ate all the food and drink they had planned to take. Tellers' versions of the story differ across the Strait.

show.text: A canoe at the shore with the crew sitting among empty food baskets.

say.text: The stars also carry practical knowledge. Islander laws, customs and practices, along with knowledge needed for survival, are handed down through story, song, dance and ceremony.

show.text:
Story · Song · Dance · Ceremony
Law · Custom · Survival knowledge

ask.q: What do the Tagai stories focus on?
ask.right: The stars. They identify Torres Strait Islanders as sea people who share a way of life.
wrong: Desert rock formations.
Mountain glaciers.
Rivers that flow inland.
ask.why: The Queensland Curriculum and Assessment Authority explains that the Tagai stories focus on the stars and identify Torres Strait Islanders as sea people.

say.text: Many Torres Strait Islanders do not see land and sea as separate. On Mabuiag, heaven is not straight up. It lies on an island called Kibu, to the northwest, and a spirit sails there at sundown.

show.text: A small sailing canoe heading toward the northwest horizon at sunset.

say.text: Now we cross the sea to Aotearoa New Zealand and the Māori. At the centre of traditional Māori religion were the atua, often called gods.

show.text: Atua

say.text: In Māori belief the natural and supernatural worlds were one, and there was no Māori word for religion. Missionaries introduced the word whakapono, which also means faith and trust.

show.text:
Māori belief | Word for it
Natural and supernatural are one | No word for 'religion'
Missionaries introduced | Whakapono (also faith, trust)

say.text: A key creation story is about Ranginui, the sky father, and Papatūānuku, the earth mother. They were locked in an embrace, and their children were trapped between them in darkness. Those children decided to try to separate their parents.

show.text: Sky father and earth mother in a tight embrace, with small figures of their children pressed between them in the dark.

say.text: The children became atua of the world's parts. Tangaroa is god of the sea, Tāne of the forest, Tāwhirimātea of the wind, and Tūmatauenga of war and people. Rongo and Haumia are gods of cultivated and uncultivated foods.

show.text:
Atua | Domain
Tangaroa | Sea
Tāne | Forest
Tāwhirimātea | Wind
Tūmatauenga | War and people
Rongo | Cultivated foods
Haumia | Uncultivated foods

ask.q: In the Māori creation story, who are Ranginui and Papatūānuku?
ask.right: The sky father and the earth mother, parents of the atua.
wrong: Two rival human kings.
The first Christian missionaries.
Two sailors who found New Zealand.
ask.why: Te Ara describes Ranginui as the sky father and Papatūānuku as the earth mother. Their children, including Tāne and Tangaroa, are the atua of the forest and sea.

say.text: Stories also say where people come from. In one telling, Tāne obtained the human aspect from the heavens and placed it in Hineahuone, the first woman. In another tradition, humans descend from the god Tiki.

show.text: Where people come from

say.text: Māori are Polynesian, and two ideas appear across Polynesia, and in parts of Melanesia and Micronesia: mana and tapu. Mana first. It is a sacred power, a state in which a person or thing is under the influence of gods or spirits.

show.text: Mana

say.text: Chiefs were believed to hold great mana. But mana was not held only by people. Buildings, stones and tools could hold it too, and it could be good or dangerous.

show.text: People · Chiefs · Buildings · Stones · Tools

say.text: Tapu is the second idea. These are rules protecting what is sacred, often glossed as 'forbidden'. Breaking a tapu was believed to bring misfortune or even death.

show.text: Tapu = sacred and set apart

say.text: You can still see this respect. In much of Polynesia it is poor manners to step over a person's legs, or to put your head higher than a person of high rank. People believe these actions sap mana.

show.text: A guest bending low as they walk past seated elders, taking care not to step over anyone's legs.

ask.q: In Polynesian traditions, what is a tapu?
ask.right: A rule that protects what is sacred and set apart, and breaking it was believed to bring misfortune.
wrong: A type of ocean canoe.
A song sung only at weddings.
A name for a human chief.
ask.why: Britannica Kids says tapu rules protected sacred things, and breaking a tapu was believed to bring misfortune or even death.

say.text: Hawaii is another Polynesian tradition. Its religion is also called the kapu system. Four gods are most often named: Kū, Kāne, Lono and Kanaloa. The formal kapu system stayed in place until 1819.

show.text: Kū · Kāne · Lono · Kanaloa

say.text: Hawaiian practice did not stop in 1819. Fishermen still observe a kapu on spawning fish. 'Aumakua, guardian ancestors who can appear as a shark, an owl or even a rock, are still honoured by some Hawaiians today.

show.text: A fisher at the edge of the sea, leaving spawning fish alone. Nearby is a carved stone of a guardian ancestor.

say.text: Micronesia is a third region of the Pacific. There is no single belief system there, because each island region has its own beings. In Chuuk, for example, a god named Anulap teaches magic and knowledge to humans.

show.text: Micronesia's island groups: the Carolines, Marshalls, Marianas and Gilberts, each with its own stories.

say.text: In Melanesia, Vanuatu has over a hundred languages across about eighty islands. Its word for traditional ways is kastom. Kastom means the whole mix of knowledge, practice, belief and social life that began before Christianity and continues alongside it.

show.text: Kastom

ask.right: The whole complex of traditional knowledge, practice, belief and social life, which continues alongside Christianity.
wrong: A type of church building.
A tax collected by the government.
A single holy book.
ask.why: The ethnotheology profile explains that kastom covers indigenous knowledge, practice, belief, social organisation and spiritual relationship. It predates Christianity and persists alongside it.

say.text: In the spiritual world of kastom there is no separate realm above or below this one. Vanuatu communities often took on Christianity in form while keeping kastom in practice.

show.text:
Christianity | Kastom
Taken up in form | Kept in practice

say.text: Some Melanesian movements are called cargo cults. In them, villagers used renewed or new rituals to ask ancestral spirits or other powerful beings to provide 'cargo', meaning goods. Scholars debate the label, as you'll see in 'The other side'.

show.text: 'Cargo' = kago, goods

say.text: Now let's look at how these traditions met Christianity. In the Torres Strait, missionaries arrived in 1871 and ended some old ways of life and the fighting between islands.

show.text: 1871: the Coming of the Light

say.text: That arrival is remembered each year on 1 July as the Coming of the Light. The London Missionary Society reached Erub that day. Today Christianity remains strong in Torres Strait communities, and a major ceremony marks the date.

show.text: A community gathering on a beach at dawn for a Coming of the Light celebration.

say.text: For Aboriginal Catholics, one Catholic source says Elders saw many likenesses between Bible stories and their own traditional stories and laws. The same source says traditional rituals, language and spirituality were suppressed or lost as people were forced to integrate.

show.text:
Similarities noticed | Losses recorded
Bible stories and traditional stories | Rituals, language and spirituality suppressed or lost

say.text: In Aotearoa, colonialism led many Māori to become Christian. It also gave rise to new Māori-centred faiths: Pai Mārire, Ringatū and later Rātana.

show.text: Pai Mārire · Ringatū · Rātana

say.text: Te Ua Haumēne developed Pai Mārire from 1862. Its name means good and peaceful. Te Kooti founded Ringatū, the upraised hand, while held on the Chatham Islands. His Bible study produced a faith that kept traditional taboos and faith healing.

show.text:
Pai Mārire | Ringatū
Founded by Te Ua Haumēne, from 1862 | Founded by Te Kooti, 1860s
'Good and peaceful' | 'The upraised hand'

say.text: Tahupōtiki Rātana was a farmer who fasted and prayed when his son became very sick. He founded a religious movement, and also a political one that held all the Māori seats in Parliament for many years.

show.text: Rātana

say.text: Here is a timeline of how some of these traditions and Christianity met.

show.text:
1819: Hawaiian kapu system formally ends
1862: Te Ua Haumēne develops Pai Mārire
1860s: Te Kooti founds Ringatū
1871: Missionaries reach Erub in the Torres Strait

say.text: What about today? In New Zealand's 2023 census, most Māori gave no religion. About 24% gave Christianity and about 7% gave Māori religions, beliefs and philosophies.

show.text: Religious affiliation of Māori people, 2023 Census

say.text: The Māori religions group in the census is mainly three faiths: Rātana, Ringatū and Pai Mārire. Two of them are new faiths, and Pai Mārire grew from the same era.

show.text: Rātana · Ringatū · Pai Mārire

ask.q: Which three faiths mainly make up the census category 'Māori religions, beliefs and philosophies'?
wrong: Shinto, Daoism and Jainism.
Hinduism, Sikhism and Buddhism.
Zoroastrianism, the Baháʼí Faith and Druze.
ask.why: The NZ Association of Rationalists and Humanists, writing about Stats NZ census results, says this group is principally Rātana, Ringatū and Pai Mārire.

say.text: In Australia the census shows a different picture. In 2016, under 2% of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people reported Australian Aboriginal traditional religions or beliefs.

show.text: Under 2%

say.text: A small number does not mean spirituality has lost its meaning. Country, culture and spirituality are described as central to the identity of many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people.

show.text: A tick-box is not the whole story

say.text: So where are these traditions practised? In Aboriginal communities across Australia and in the Torres Strait Islands. They are also practised in Aotearoa, Hawaiʻi and Vanuatu, often alongside Christianity.

show.text: A map of Australia, the Torres Strait, New Zealand, Hawaiʻi and Vanuatu, each marked as a place where these traditions continue.

say.text: Let's pull it together. Stories explain the world and carry law. Land is a living relative with responsibilities. Ancestors, spirits and atua connect people to both.

show.text:
Story: explains the world and carries law
Land: Country, with responsibilities
Ancestors: connect people to story and land

ask.q: Which sentence best sums up how land works in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander spirituality?
ask.right: Land, or Country, is tied to ancestors and stories, and it carries responsibilities.
wrong: Land is only a resource to be sold.
Land has no connection to ancestors or stories.
Land only matters in the distant past.
ask.why: Study Australia says Country includes land, water, animals, plants and people. It adds that connection to land brings responsibilities in Aboriginal law, honoured through ceremony.

say.text: Next time, in class sixteen, we look at newer movements and non-religious worldviews. If you want to learn whose Country you are on, Study Australia points to the AIATSIS website.

show.text: Next: Newer Movements and Non-Religious Worldviews

frame_of_reference.elsewhere: Farming villages were spreading across West Asia and other parts of the world. In the Torres Strait, rising seas were flooding the land bridge to Papua New Guinea. Islander culture stretches back to around then.
Singapore was founded as a British trading post. In Hawaii, the formal kapu system came to an end.
The American Civil War was fought, and Japan's Meiji Restoration began in 1868. In New Zealand, Pai Mārire developed from 1862 and Te Kooti founded Ringatū in the mid-1860s.
The German Empire was proclaimed. In the Torres Strait, missionaries reached Erub, an event Islanders remember as the Coming of the Light.

other_side.claim: Some accounts say Māori traditionally believed in one supreme god, Io.
other_side.other_view: Te Ara explains that some people have searched early manuscripts for evidence of Io. Others think the idea of Io came from the Christian idea of God, and they argue there is no concrete evidence of Io in early Māori traditions. Te Rangi Hīroa, a Māori scholar, wrote that the discovery of a supreme god named Io was a surprise to both Māori and Pākehā.

other_side.claim: 'Cargo cults' are simply attempts to get goods by magic.
other_side.other_view: Anthropologists have given many explanations for these movements, including greed, deep Melanesian religious beliefs, and colonial inequality and oppression. One scholar writing about Vanuatu's Tanna argues that 'cargo cult' is a Western projection and not a Melanesian reality. Others call such movements forerunners of Melanesian nationalism.

other_side.claim: The census shows that traditional Aboriginal religion is almost gone.
other_side.other_view: The 2016 census found under 2% of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people reporting traditional religions. Other sources describe Country, culture and spirituality as central to the identity of many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people. A census tick-box measures what people choose to list as a religion, so it may not capture everything. This last point is the class's own inference.

other_side.claim: Missionaries simply ended old ways in the Torres Strait.
other_side.other_view: Queensland's education authority says missionaries put an end to some old ways of life and to fighting between islands. Torres Strait Islanders of all faiths gather each year to mark the Coming of the Light, and the QCAA says Christianity remains strong in Torres Strait communities.
